name: Uranus Discovered (1781)
teaser: William Herschel, an amateur astronomer and music teacher, found a new planet while sweeping the night sky with a homemade telescope — the first planet discovered in recorded history, and the first never known to the ancients.

exploreAction.targetName: Herschel's 1781 paper 'Account of a Comet' (Philosophical Transactions)
exploreAction.instruction: Herschel at first thought he had found a comet, because no one had imagined another planet. Read how his report to the Royal Society was titled 'Account of a Comet' — and how the orbit calculations by others proved it was a planet, doubling the size of the known solar system overnight.

name: Ceres, the First Asteroid (1801)
teaser: Giuseppe Piazzi spotted a faint moving star on New Year's Eve 1801 and lost it in the glare of the sun weeks later. Gauss, then 24, used his new method of orbit determination to predict where it would reappear — and it was found exactly where he said.

exploreAction.targetName: The story of Ceres's rediscovery via Gauss's orbit calculation
exploreAction.instruction: Piazzi found Ceres between Mars and Jupiter — filling a gap the astronomer Titius had predicted. It was called a 'missing planet,' then demoted to asteroid when more appeared. Today we call it a dwarf planet. Notice how this discovery made Gauss famous and launched celestial mechanics.

name: Pluto Discovered (1930)
teaser: After a decade-long photographic hunt for 'Planet X,' a 23-year-old farm boy from Kansas — Clyde Tombaugh — found a faint moving dot by blinking glass plates under a microscope. The name Pluto was suggested by an 11-year-old English schoolgirl.

exploreAction.targetName: The discovery plates and story of the 1930 Pluto hunt at Lowell Observatory
exploreAction.instruction: Tombaugh compared pairs of photographs of the same sky taken nights apart, looking for any star that had moved. He found Pluto in January 1930 after nearly a year of scanning. Read about the 'blink comparator' method and why the planet was later reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

name: Quasars Identified (1963)
teaser: Radio astronomers found objects that looked like stars but screamed in radio; when Maarten Schmidt took the spectrum of 3C 273, the pattern of lines was redshifted an impossible 16% — meaning this 'star' was billions of light-years away and blazing with the light of a trillion suns.

exploreAction.targetName: Schmidt's 1963 Nature paper on the spectrum of 3C 273
exploreAction.instruction: The key move was recognizing Balmer hydrogen lines in 3C 273's spectrum, hugely redshifted. That redshift meant distance — and distance meant luminosity beyond anything known. Read about the puzzle 'quasi-stellar radio sources' posed, and how they turned out to be supermassive black holes feeding at the centers of young galaxies.

name: Cygnus X-1, the First Black Hole (1964)
teaser: A rocket-borne X-ray detector found a brilliant X-ray source in Cygnus in 1964, but it took years to prove what it was: a star being cannibalized by a dark, invisible companion too heavy to be a neutron star. It became the first widely accepted black hole.

exploreAction.targetName: The story of Cygnus X-1's identification as a black hole
exploreAction.instruction: Cygnus X-1 emits X-rays because gas ripped from its blue supergiant companion spirals into the black hole and heats to millions of degrees. Stephen Hawking famously bet against its being a black hole — and conceded in 1990. Read how astronomers measured the invisible companion's mass to prove its nature.

name: Gamma-Ray Bursts (1967)
teaser: Cold War spy satellites built to watch for nuclear tests instead caught short, brilliant flashes of gamma rays from deep space. For 25 years nobody knew what they were — some of the most powerful explosions in the universe, and for a long time the biggest mystery in astronomy.

exploreAction.targetName: The discovery of gamma-ray bursts by the Vela satellites
exploreAction.instruction: The Vela satellites were classified military hardware; the bursts were declassified in 1973. Read how the debate raged over whether bursts came from our galaxy or cosmological distances — settled in 1997 when one burst's afterglow was caught and its redshift measured. They are now understood as collapsing massive stars.

name: The Kuiper Belt (1992)
teaser: For decades astronomers suspected a band of icy debris beyond Neptune, but couldn't find it. In 1992, David Jewitt and Jane Luu spent a night on a telescope that could barely find it, and found the first one: 1992 QB1, a 200-kilometer iceball 40 times farther from the sun than Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: The pair had searched for years, imaging the same patches of sky and blinking for movement. The discovery of QB1 opened the floodgates: thousands of Kuiper Belt objects are now known, and Pluto is understood as just the largest of them. Read how the search was done and why it took so long.

name: Uranus's Rings (1977)
teaser: Astronomers watching Uranus pass in front of a star noticed the star blink five times before and after the occultation — the signature of thin rings around a planet no one expected to have them. It was a lucky accident: the whole crew was aboard a plane for the observation.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1977 stellar occultation observations of Uranus's rings
exploreAction.instruction: The team flew aboard the Kuiper Airborne Observatory to watch Uranus occult a star. The star's light blinked off and on symmetrically around the planet — rings! Read how the discovery forced a rethink, and how Voyager 2 later photographed the thin, dark ring system in 1986.

name: Charon, Pluto's Moon (1978)
teaser: Jim Christy noticed that Pluto's image in a telescope photograph had a suspicious bump. It turned out to be a moon — half Pluto's size, orbiting so tightly that Pluto and Charon are sometimes called a double planet. The discovery let astronomers weigh Pluto for the first time.

exploreAction.targetName: Christy's 1978 discovery announcement of Pluto's satellite
exploreAction.instruction: The bump appeared on plates taken for Pluto's orbit refinement. Christy named the moon after his wife Charlene ('Char'), and the mythological ferryman happened to fit perfectly. Read how Charon's orbit gave Pluto's mass — far smaller than anyone had assumed — which later fed the debate over Pluto's planethood.

name: Tycho's Supernova (1572)
teaser: A new star blazed in Cassiopeia, brighter than Venus, visible in daylight. Tycho Brahe measured its position obsessively and proved it lay beyond the moon — demolishing the Aristotelian belief that the heavens never change. It was a supernova, a star's death seen from 7,500 light-years away.

exploreAction.instruction: Tycho showed the 'nova' had no parallax — meaning it was farther away than the moon — by comparing its position with nearby stars night after night. Read his account, the book that made him famous, and consider how it cracked the perfect, unchanging heavens. The remnant's light echoes were finally imaged in 2008.

name: Kepler's Supernova (1604)
teaser: The last supernova seen with the naked eye in our galaxy exploded in 1604, and Kepler watched it for a year, publishing detailed observations. It happened just 32 years after Tycho's star — and none has been seen in the Milky Way since, though many must have occurred.

exploreAction.instruction: Kepler's book mixed careful astronomy with astrology — he interpreted the star as a portent. Read his account of the star's brightness changes and colors. Modern astronomers found the remnant's X-ray and radio emission and identified the explosion as a Type Ia supernova, a white dwarf that detonated.

name: Supernova 1987A (1987)
teaser: On February 23, 1987, a star exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud — the nearest supernova in 400 years. Neutrinos from the blast were detected on Earth three hours before the light arrived, opening a new way of watching the universe.

exploreAction.instruction: Ian Shelton, an assistant at Las Campanas, noticed the bright star on a routine plate — it wasn't there before. The neutrino detectors Kamiokande and IMB registered a handful of neutrinos minutes earlier. Read how 1987A confirmed the theory that massive stars explode and forge heavy elements.

name: Helium Found on the Sun (1868)
teaser: During a total solar eclipse, astronomers saw a bright yellow line in the sun's spectrum that matched nothing on Earth. They named the mystery element after Helios, the Greek sun god — and it took 27 years before helium was found on Earth. The first element discovered in space.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1868 eclipse observations that revealed helium
exploreAction.instruction: Pierre Janssen observed the eclipse from India and noticed the yellow line even without an eclipse; Norman Lockyer, in England, attributed it to an unknown element. Read how the line was labeled D3 and how Ramsay finally isolated helium on Earth in 1895, from a uranium mineral.

name: The Neutrino Detected (1956)
teaser: In 1930, Wolfgang Pauli invented the neutrino — a ghost particle with no charge and almost no mass — just to balance the books in beta decay, apologizing that he had done something no theorist should do: propose a particle that could never be detected. In 1956, it was.

exploreAction.instruction: Cowan and Reines placed huge tanks of water next to a nuclear reactor, which floods out antineutrinos. A neutrino hitting a proton produces a positron and a neutron, and they caught the telltale pair of flashes. Read how they used 200 liters of water and cadmium-loaded liquid, and why Pauli's 'impossible' particle won a Nobel in 1995.

name: The Positron (1932)
teaser: Carl Anderson, photographing cosmic rays in a cloud chamber, found a particle with the mass of an electron but bending the wrong way in a magnetic field — antimatter, predicted by Dirac's equations four years earlier. He had discovered the first particle of antimatter.

exploreAction.instruction: The cloud chamber photo showed a thin track curving as an electron would — but opposite. Anderson at first suspected a proton, but the track was too light. Read how he had to think carefully about the direction of the track, and how this accidental discovery earned the 1936 Nobel. Antimatter had been a theory; now it was real.

name: The Muon (1936)
teaser: Cosmic-ray researchers found a particle heavier than the electron but lighter than the proton — and were deeply confused. The physicist I. I. Rabi famously asked, 'Who ordered that?' The muon was the first hint that the particle zoo would be far richer than anyone imagined.

exploreAction.targetName: The discovery of the muon in cosmic rays (1936–37)
exploreAction.instruction: Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer measured cosmic-ray tracks in cloud chambers and found particles too penetrating to be electrons. It took two years of careful work to establish the new particle's mass. Read how the muon, a 'second-generation' particle, later became key evidence for the standard model's families of matter.

name: The Tau Lepton (1975)
teaser: Martin Perl's team at SLAC found a third, much heavier cousin of the electron — the tau, 3,500 times the electron's mass. It was the first particle of a whole new 'third generation' of matter, and it decays so fast it exists for a trillionth of a trillionth of a second.

exploreAction.targetName: Perl's 1975 discovery of the tau lepton at SLAC
exploreAction.instruction: Perl's team collided electrons and positrons and looked for events where a muon and an electron appeared together — a signature no known process could explain. Read how the tau was hidden among thousands of events, and how it completed the three generations of leptons in the standard model.

name: Sagittarius A*, the Milky Way's Black Hole (2002)
teaser: For decades astronomers suspected a black hole lurks at the center of our galaxy. In 2002, Reinhard Genzel's team completed a decade of watching stars orbit the invisible object Sgr A* — clocking one star whipping around it at 3% of light speed — proving a 4-million-solar-mass black hole is there.

exploreAction.targetName: The stellar-orbit observations of Sagittarius A*
exploreAction.instruction: Genzel and Ghez independently used adaptive optics on the infrared sky to track stars in the galactic center. The star S2 completes an orbit every 16 years, and its path traces out a perfect Kepler ellipse around an empty point. Read how these orbits yielded the black hole's mass — and won the 2020 Nobel.

name: The Moon's Far Side Photographed (1959)
teaser: The Soviet probe Luna 3 flew around the moon and radioed back the first photographs of the side no one had ever seen — a hemisphere of battered highlands, almost no maria. It was the first time humanity saw the back of another world.

exploreAction.targetName: The Luna 3 mission and its first far-side photographs
exploreAction.instruction: The spacecraft took 29 photos on film, developed them on board, and transmitted them by radio — a technical tour de force in 1959. Read how the far side's lack of dark maria reshaped theories of lunar formation, and how the 'dark side' myth persists despite the far side getting just as much sunlight.
